To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
insulin administered in CAP-PEG particles by spray instillation to rats is more bioavailable and has a slower rate of elimination than that administered in solution.
the presence of CAP- and PEG-containing particles in the lungs of rats increases systemic insulin bioavailability.
the presence of CAP and PEG particles appears to positively affect the disposition of insulin in rats after pulmonary administration.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a pulmonary insulin delivery system for the treatment of diabetes mellitus in humans.
the design of novel particles for pulmonary delivery of insulin and the investigation of their PK/PD properties.
the development of a pulmonary delivery system for insulin that is capable of providing sustained release.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
insulin-CAP-PEG particle administration by the spray route was the most effective pulmonary method of insulin delivery in the rat model.
the presence of CAP-PE particles and spray instillation positively influence the disposition and bioavailability of insulin administered to rats by the pulmonary route.
the use of insulin-CAP-PEG nanoparticles administered by pulmonary spray instillation may be an efficient and effective method of insulin delivery.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the combination of CAP and PEG in particles is a useful strategy for the pulmonary delivery of insulin.
the use of CAP-PEG microparticles as a pulmonary delivery system for insulin in rats is an effective method to prolong insulin action and to reduce insulin-induced hypoglycemia.

the combination of CAP and PEG in particles is an effective means of delivering insulin to rat lungs, and spray administration is an efficient method of administering particles to the lungs of these animals.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of CAP-PEGS particles in suspension positively influences the PK and PD profiles of insulin administered to rats by the pulmonary route.
the use of CAP-PEG insulin particles for inhalation therapy may be a viable option for the treatment of diabetes mellitus.
the presence of CAP-PE particles in suspension can enhance the pulmonary absorption of insulin in rats.
